scenario: A grant panel could ask members to disclose ties to applicants before reviewing proposals, then decide whether each connection requires recusal or another safeguard.

title: Recusal
source_title: 28 U.S. Code § 455: Disqualification of justice, judge, or magistrate judge
publisher: Cornell Legal Information Institute / US Code
finding: Recusal removes a decision-maker from a matter when involvement threatens impartiality or creates a specified conflict. US judicial disqualification law illustrates both a general impartiality test and particular relationships or interests requiring withdrawal.
limitation: The statute governs US federal judges and includes exceptions; organizational recusal policies require their own criteria and replacement decision procedures.
scenario: A hiring committee member whose close relative applies could withdraw from reviewing that application, with the remaining panel recording the recusal and following its agreed procedure.

title: Appeals procedures
publisher: Administrative Office of the US Courts
finding: Appeal procedures allow a decision to be reviewed by another authorized body through defined grounds and submissions. Federal appellate practice illustrates structured review using briefs and sometimes oral argument rather than simply repeating the original decision.
limitation: The judicial example is jurisdiction-specific; appeal rights, review standards, deadlines, and whether new evidence is allowed differ across systems.
scenario: A professional association could let disciplined members appeal to a separate panel, specifying acceptable grounds, submission deadlines, and whether the panel may overturn or return decisions.

title: Ombuds offices
source_title: Comparison Table for IOA Standards of Practice
finding: An organizational ombuds provides an independent, impartial, confidential, and informal place to discuss concerns. The standards describe listening, clarifying issues, developing options, and sometimes facilitating informal intervention without replacing formal organizational decision channels.
limitation: The cited document explains organizational ombuds practice; statutory ombuds may have different powers, and confidentiality or informality can have defined exceptions.
scenario: A university could provide an ombuds office where a student confidentially explores a departmental dispute and learns available options before deciding whether to file a formal complaint.

title: Sunset clauses
source_title: Explanatory Memorandum: Product Safety and Metrology amendment regulations
finding: A sunset clause gives a rule or authorization an explicit expiry point rather than allowing indefinite continuation by default. The explanatory memorandum illustrates using a sunset provision to end a temporary recognition arrangement.
limitation: The source is a specific legislative example; expiry does not itself ensure evaluation, and replacement or renewal procedures must be specified separately.
scenario: A committee could authorize a temporary spending exception for three months, stating that it expires unless members review the experience and explicitly renew it.

title: Public decision records
publisher: Charity Commission for England and Wales
finding: Decision records preserve what was decided, the reasons, supporting information, attendance, and declared conflicts. Charity meeting guidance illustrates minutes as an accountable record and requires access for specified organizational audiences rather than a verbatim transcript.
limitation: The source supports recordkeeping and member access, not universal public disclosure; privacy, governing documents, and jurisdiction affect what may be published.
scenario: A cooperative could publish a redacted decision log showing resolutions and reasons, while retaining a fuller internal record for sensitive personnel or contractual matters.

title: Emergency authority with limits
source_title: France: Final Opinion on Article 49.3 of the Constitution
finding: Emergency authority can temporarily concentrate powers for exceptional conditions while limiting their subject matter and duration. The Venice Commission emphasizes a legal basis, relevance to the emergency, and expiry unless the legislature confirms continuation.
limitation: This constitutional guidance concerns government powers; emergency labels do not justify unlimited scope, and actual safeguards depend on enforceable review arrangements.
scenario: An association could authorize a crisis coordinator to make urgent safety expenditures for one week, requiring documented decisions and a board vote for any extension.

title: Commons-based peer production
source_title: Coase's Penguin, or, Linux and the Nature of the Firm
finding: Commons-based peer production coordinates contributions to shared resources without relying solely on employer commands or market transactions. Benkler develops the concept through networked projects whose outputs remain broadly available for others to use and improve.
limitation: This theoretical account explains an organizational form; openness alone does not solve integration, maintenance, participation inequality, or sustainable funding.
scenario: A community could build an openly reusable map, allowing volunteers to choose tasks while maintainers define contribution standards and combine contributions into a coherent shared resource.

title: Project teams
finding: Project teams assemble people around a defined undertaking with a beginning, an end, and a distinct output. The paper examines how temporary collaboration can also develop shared knowledge and connections between participants' established professional communities.
limitation: The paper explores project teams as learning entities; a temporary assignment does not automatically produce shared understanding or preserve learning afterward.
scenario: An association could assemble a temporary team to launch a new library, define its deliverable and completion date, and document lessons before disbanding.

title: Working groups
finding: Working groups concentrate continuing discussion and production around a defined problem or deliverable. IETF groups illustrate charters, facilitated public discussion, document editors, and consensus processes that connect individual contributions to a collectively maintained specification.
limitation: This describes the IETF's open technical process; other working groups may have restricted membership, different authority, or less formal output expectations.
scenario: A standards association could charter a working group to draft accessibility guidance, define its remit, and use a public discussion archive to develop revisions.

title: Task forces
source_title: ICS Position Training: Foundations Course Reference Guide
finding: Task forces combine different kinds of resources for a particular mission or operational need. FEMA's incident-management definition requires a designated leader and common communications, making the mixed resources usable as a coordinated unit.
limitation: The cited definition belongs to incident command; applying it to ordinary organizational task forces requires adapting authority, duration, and reporting arrangements.
scenario: After severe storm damage, a municipality could assemble a temporary debris task force combining public works, transport, and utility personnel under one coordinator and communication plan.

title: Cross-functional teams
finding: Cross-functional teams bring together the skills needed to complete an outcome within one team. The Scrum Guide describes collective capability, reducing dependence on passing each stage of a deliverable through separately managed specialist groups.
limitation: The source describes Scrum teams; cross-functionality means combined team capability, not that every member is equally skilled in every discipline.
scenario: A service redesign team could include operations, design, engineering, and customer support so it can test a complete improvement rather than queue work across departments.

title: Guilds across teams
finding: Cross-team guilds connect people with a shared professional interest across their normal delivery teams. The Spotify account describes voluntary communities for exchanging practices and knowledge without replacing the teams responsible for day-to-day work.
limitation: This is a historical practitioner snapshot, not a universal organizational model; a guild's authority and participation incentives need separate clarification.
scenario: Designers scattered across product teams could form a monthly guild to compare accessibility practices, share reusable examples, and propose improvements without taking over product decisions.

title: Hackathons
finding: Hackathons reserve a short, defined period for participants to explore problems and build prototypes together. The playbook distinguishes learning, exploration, prototyping, and validation goals and stresses documenting results and deciding what deserves follow-up.
limitation: This practitioner guide focuses on internal AI events; a prototype is not a production-ready service or evidence of lasting organizational adoption.
scenario: A civic group could run a weekend hackathon to prototype tools for local accessibility problems, then select one promising idea for further testing with residents.

title: Sprints
finding: Sprints organize work into repeating, fixed-length periods with a goal, delivery effort, and opportunities to inspect and adapt. In Scrum, each sprint lasts no more than a month and contains planning, review, and retrospective activities.
limitation: The guide defines Scrum practice, not every use of the word sprint; a deadline alone does not create its feedback cycle.
scenario: A team could work toward one demonstrable improvement over two weeks, review it with users, and use a retrospective to adjust the next sprint.

title: Work parties
source_title: Practical Conservation: Leeds Midweek Practical Team
finding: Work parties gather participants for a scheduled block of practical collective work. The conservation example coordinates a meeting place, transport, equipment expectations, and a shared task so volunteers can contribute together without taking permanent roles.
limitation: This event listing illustrates the arrangement rather than measuring outcomes; practical tasks still require suitable supervision, permissions, equipment, and accessibility planning.
scenario: Neighbors could organize a Saturday work party to restore a shared garden, arranging tools, task supervision, refreshments, and clear arrival and finish times.

title: Barn-raising
publisher: Elizabethtown College Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies
finding: Barn-raising concentrates community labor on a substantial construction task that would overwhelm a household alone. The Amish example places this coordinated effort within reciprocal mutual aid, including rebuilding after disasters and supporting members in need.
limitation: The source describes a particular religious community's practices; transferring the format does not transfer its relationships, construction expertise, or obligations.
scenario: A rural community could organize skilled volunteers to help rebuild a neighbor's damaged outbuilding, coordinating materials and supervision while treating safety and necessary approvals as prerequisites.

title: Pair work
publisher: Birgitta Böckeler and Nina Siessegger / MartinFowler.com
finding: Pair work puts two people on one task with complementary attention. Pair programming's driver and navigator roles illustrate one person handling immediate execution while the other reviews, anticipates problems, and considers the broader direction.
limitation: The source concerns programming; pairing styles require adaptation, and differences in confidence or experience can turn collaboration into one person's domination.
scenario: Two colleagues could draft a difficult proposal together, alternating between writing and reviewing assumptions so both understand the argument and can challenge weak sections.

title: Mob or ensemble work
finding: Ensemble work has a whole team collaborate on one work item at the same time, sharing execution and review. The mob programming example extends pairing to design, coding, testing, and other coordinated development work.
limitation: The description is a practitioner approach, not proof of universal productivity gains; participation, facilitation, fatigue, and task suitability influence the experience.
scenario: A software team could tackle an unfamiliar integration together around one shared workspace, discussing choices and rotating execution so knowledge remains distributed across the team.

title: Shared task boards
finding: Shared task boards make work items and their movement through agreed states visible. The Kanban Guide connects this visualization to explicit definitions of starting, finishing, and workflow policies rather than prescribing a particular board layout.
limitation: A board can expose work without resolving overload; its usefulness depends on current information and shared definitions of each state.
scenario: A volunteer team could display requests as waiting, active, blocked, and finished, reviewing blocked items together so help goes where progress has stalled.

title: Work-in-progress limits
finding: Work-in-progress controls limit how many items occupy a workflow or stage. New work is pulled when capacity becomes available, making finishing and unblocking existing work part of the decision to begin anything else.
limitation: Limits need agreed exceptions and context-sensitive adjustment; reducing the number of active items does not guarantee faster delivery under every constraint.
scenario: A support team could allow at most five active investigations, helping finish or unblock one before accepting another item into that stage.

title: Issue triage
finding: Issue triage evaluates incoming reports before they enter the working backlog. GitHub's intake example distinguishes actionable issues from those needing more information, making clarification and classification part of maintaining usable shared work records.
limitation: The cited implementation uses AI assistance; it supports the intake mechanism, not a requirement to automate or trust classifications without review.
scenario: Maintainers could review new bug reports weekly, request missing reproduction details, and distinguish actionable problems from incomplete submissions before scheduling development work.

title: Request-for-comments processes
finding: A request-for-comments process asks contributors to write substantial proposed changes before implementation and expose them to discussion. Rust's process uses feedback, alternatives, and drawbacks to refine proposals and support an explicit decision about adoption.
limitation: The source defines one project's governance; an RFC is neither automatic approval nor necessarily an Internet standards document.
scenario: An open project could require a written proposal for a major compatibility change, giving contributors time to examine alternatives before maintainers decide whether implementation should proceed.

title: Design reviews
source_title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook: Life-Cycle Reviews
finding: Design reviews create checkpoints where a proposed design is examined against requirements, risks, interfaces, and constraints before further commitment. NASA's preliminary design review asks whether the evidence supports moving into detailed design.
limitation: NASA's spaceflight context is demanding and specialized; copying its full review apparatus may burden smaller projects without proportionate benefit.
scenario: A team designing a community facility could review accessibility, operating costs, and unresolved interfaces before commissioning detailed plans, documenting issues that must be resolved first.

title: Release governance
finding: Release governance separates creating a candidate from authorizing an official release. Apache's example assigns a release manager, establishes approval voting, and controls official artifacts and announcements so publication carries a recognizable project's endorsement.
limitation: These are one project's rules, not universal open-source requirements; a release vote does not guarantee that every defect has been found.
scenario: An open-source project could designate a release coordinator, invite testing of a candidate, and require its maintainers' recorded approval before publishing an official version.

title: Standards bodies
finding: Standards bodies convene experts and affected interests to negotiate shared specifications. ISO describes proposals responding to a recognized need, technical committees developing scope and content, and a consensus process that considers stakeholder comments.
limitation: ISO describes its formal process; participation does not automatically remove unequal resources or make a resulting standard mandatory in law.
scenario: Manufacturers, users, and accessibility advocates could work through a standards body to agree a common connector specification so independently produced devices can work together.

title: Protocols and interfaces
source_title: RFC 1958: Architectural Principles of the Internet
finding: Protocols specify shared rules that independently implemented systems follow when exchanging information. The Internet architecture guidance emphasizes consistent specifications and terminology, illustrating how agreed interfaces can coordinate separate implementations without dictating their entire internal design.
limitation: The source concerns technical networking; using protocols as a social coordination analogy requires defining human responsibilities, exceptions, and interpretation explicitly.
scenario: Several partner organizations could agree a common referral format and acknowledgement procedure so requests move between them reliably while each retains its own internal workflow.

title: Standard operating procedures
source_title: Guidance for Preparing Standard Operating Procedures
finding: Standard operating procedures document repeatable work as clear, ordered steps with an identified scope, approval, and revision history. EPA guidance stresses tailoring detail to the activity and making instructions understandable to appropriately knowledgeable users.
limitation: The guide supports consistency, not infallibility; obsolete instructions, unusual conditions, or inadequate training can make routine compliance insufficient.
scenario: A community laboratory could document equipment setup and shutdown, assign responsibility for approving updates, and review the procedure when equipment or working conditions change.

title: Checklists
source_title: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: Tools and resources
finding: Checklists externalize critical reminders and create moments for coordinated confirmation. WHO's surgical example asks team members to pause and verbally verify items using a reference tool, making the checklist a communication process as well as a memory aid.
limitation: The source concerns surgical safety; benefits in another setting cannot be assumed, and mechanical box-ticking can miss the intended team discussion.
scenario: An event crew could use a short pre-opening checklist to confirm exits, communications, and assigned responsibilities together before admitting visitors to the venue.

title: Handoff protocols
publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
finding: Handoff protocols structure the transfer of information, responsibility, and accountability between people. TeamSTEPPS guidance requires the receiver to recognize the transfer and gives both parties opportunities to clarify uncertainty, ask questions, and review the plan.
limitation: The source concerns clinical teamwork; adapting it elsewhere requires choosing relevant information and confirming that the receiving person has actual authority.
scenario: A support volunteer ending a shift could brief the incoming volunteer on unresolved cases, confirm who now owns each action, and allow questions before leaving.

title: Responsibility matrices
source_title: PMI Lexicon of Project Management Terms
finding: Responsibility matrices map project work to the people or resources assigned to it. The PMI definition treats the matrix as a grid linking work packages and resources, making assignment visible across the project.
limitation: The cited definition supports assignment mapping; it does not prescribe a particular RACI variant or prove that documenting ownership resolves conflict.
scenario: A festival team could map venue booking, volunteer scheduling, and ticketing to named owners, reviewing gaps or overlaps before tasks begin falling between teams.

title: Service-level agreements
finding: Service-level agreements specify the service a provider promises, measurable performance targets, and what happens when commitments are missed. The explanation includes responsibilities, exclusions, and escalation arrangements alongside metrics such as availability or response time.
limitation: This is a provider's explanatory guide; contractual force and remedies depend on actual terms, and a target is not a guarantee.
scenario: A shared-services team and its partner organizations could agree response-time commitments, escalation contacts, measurement methods, and exclusions before relying on the service for daily work.

title: Rotating duty rosters
finding: Duty rosters assign time-bounded responsibility for attending to a shared service or recurring need. Google's on-call guidance illustrates rotating coverage, explicit shift lengths, and attention to workload so responsibility remains identifiable across time.
limitation: The source concerns engineering operations; fair rotation alone does not ensure sufficient staffing, recovery time, training, or manageable interruption rates.
scenario: A community venue could rotate opening-duty shifts among trained volunteers, publish a backup contact, and review whether unpopular shifts are being distributed fairly.

title: Incident command
source_title: NIMS Overview for Senior Officials: Instructor Guide
finding: Incident command creates an expandable coordination structure matched to an incident's size, complexity, and hazards. FEMA's model activates needed functions and assigns someone in charge of each, rather than requiring the full structure for every event.
limitation: This is an emergency-management framework; authority, training, and interagency arrangements must be established rather than improvised from an organizational chart alone.
scenario: A multi-agency exercise could practice expanding from a single incident coordinator to separate operations and logistics roles as a fictional emergency grows more complex.

title: Blameless postmortems
source_title: Lessons Learned from Other Industries: Postmortem Culture
finding: Blameless postmortems examine what happened, how the response worked, and what changes could prevent recurrence without centering personal accusation. Google's account includes publishing lessons across teams and assigning follow-up actions to turn investigation into organizational learning.
limitation: The source describes a practitioner culture, not a guarantee of candor; avoiding blame should not mean avoiding responsibility for corrective work.
scenario: After a failed event registration launch, a team could reconstruct decisions and conditions, identify missing safeguards, and assign improvements without treating one person's mistake as the explanation.

title: Communities of contribution
finding: Communities of contribution make participation in a shared project easier through welcoming interactions, accessible entry tasks, and paths toward sustained responsibility. The open-source guide describes movement from users to contributors and, potentially, maintainers.
limitation: The source offers contributor-development practices, not a standardized governance form; welcoming newcomers does not automatically distribute decision power or maintenance labor.
scenario: A neighborhood data project could offer small documented tasks, acknowledge first contributions, and invite reliable contributors into maintenance roles as their interests and capacity grow.

title: Volunteer matching
source_title: Your next steps to apply for a UN Volunteer assignment
finding: Volunteer matching connects defined assignments with people whose skills, interests, and availability fit the work. UNV's platform illustrates profiles, descriptions, applications, and selection rather than assuming goodwill alone identifies an appropriate contribution.
limitation: The source describes UNV's recruitment process; matching does not establish suitability without assessment or eliminate onboarding, supervision, and accessibility needs.
scenario: A mutual-aid network could list translation tasks with language requirements and expected time, then match interested volunteers whose availability fits the project's deadlines.

title: Time-boxed commitments
finding: Time-boxed commitments define an assignment's task, deliverable, and maximum duration before participation begins. UNV's online volunteering rules illustrate a bounded engagement with weekly hour limits and a formal conclusion acknowledging the volunteer's contribution.
limitation: This is a particular volunteering program's design, not proof that short commitments improve retention; unfinished work still needs an explicit handover plan.
scenario: A community archive could ask a volunteer to digitize a specified collection over six weeks, agreeing an hours ceiling and how remaining work will be handed over.

title: Public pledges
finding: Pledges make an intended commitment explicit, potentially connecting behavior to a stated norm. The review distinguishes honesty oaths or pledges from commitments to particular people or groups, finding these commitment types can have different behavioral effects.
limitation: The evidence concerns dishonest behavior, not every public pledge; it does not establish that publicity itself reliably improves follow-through on unrelated goals.
scenario: A group organizing a shared project could invite voluntary, specific commitments to report expenses honestly, then pair those statements with transparent records and practical review procedures.

title: Accountability partners
finding: Accountability partners agree to check in about self-chosen goals and progress. Columbia's writing guide combines specific commitments with encouragement and realistic planning, allowing the partner to support follow-through without becoming the person's supervisor.
limitation: The guide addresses writing practice and provides advice rather than experimental evidence; pressure without trust or realistic goals may undermine useful support.
scenario: Two friends could set a weekly check-in about personal writing projects, each choosing a modest goal and discussing what helped or obstructed progress.

title: Coworking sessions
finding: Coworking sessions create a shared appointment for people to work on their own tasks. Focusmate's format opens with stated goals, continues with quiet work, and closes with a brief report on what each participant accomplished.
limitation: The source describes a commercial service's format, not independent effectiveness evidence; preferences about video, privacy, and social pressure differ.
scenario: Two remote workers could meet online for fifty minutes, announce separate tasks, work quietly, and finish by sharing what they completed and what remains.

title: Distributed campaigns
finding: Distributed campaigns connect locally led groups through common principles and occasional shared actions. The 350 network illustrates local organizing aligned with a wider mission, shared visibility, and participation in national or global campaign moments.
limitation: This is one movement's organizing model; affiliation does not eliminate coordination costs, unequal capacity, or disagreements between local priorities and shared campaigns.
scenario: Local climate groups could organize actions suited to their towns while coordinating a common campaign date, shared demands, and a public directory for new participants.

title: Coalitions
source_title: Coalition Building I: Starting a Coalition
publisher: University of Kansas Community Tool Box
finding: Coalitions bring individuals or organizations together around a shared objective while retaining their separate identities. The Community Tool Box describes pooling resources, communicating across groups, and developing an action plan around a recognized common need.
limitation: The guide describes organizing practice rather than guaranteed impact; partners may differ in power, priorities, resources, and willingness to sustain participation.
scenario: Tenant groups, disability advocates, and neighborhood associations could form a coalition for accessible housing, agreeing shared demands while continuing their distinct local organizing.

title: Collective impact partnerships
publisher: FSG / John Kania and Mark Kramer
finding: Collective impact structures collaboration among organizations through a common agenda, shared measurement, complementary activities, continuing communication, and dedicated coordinating support. The original framework treats this coordination capacity as distinct from occasional partnership meetings.
limitation: The source proposes a framework rather than proving all five conditions cause success; representation, power, and measurement choices require scrutiny.
scenario: Schools, libraries, and youth organizations could coordinate a literacy initiative, agree shared outcomes, divide complementary tasks, and resource a small team to maintain communication.

title: Boundary-spanning roles
source_title: The active client: The boundary-spanning roles of internal consultants
publisher: Organization / Andrew Sturdy and Christopher Wright
finding: Boundary-spanning roles connect groups that otherwise have different knowledge, practices, or access. The study identifies internal consultants acting as gatekeepers, brokers, and partners in relationships with external consultants and the knowledge they bring.
limitation: This study concerns consultancy relationships; boundary spanners can filter or control access as well as connect groups, so their incentives matter.
scenario: A hospital could assign a liaison to translate between clinicians and software vendors, making needs understandable while documenting which concerns are being prioritized or excluded.

title: Auctions
finding: Auctions turn competing valuations into an allocation through specified bidding and payment rules. Open ascending bids, descending prices, and sealed bids expose different information and create different incentives for participants.
limitation: The best format depends on information, competition, and objectives; bidders can misjudge value or coordinate against the organizer.
scenario: Imagine a neighborhood association selling donated furniture: it announces ascending bids and a closing time, then uses the proceeds to repair its shared courtyard.

title: Double auctions
source_title: Constructivist and Ecological Rationality in Economics
finding: A double auction lets both buyers and sellers submit offers, with trades occurring when acceptable prices meet. Smith's experimental markets examined how repeated interaction can coordinate dispersed valuations without a central price setter.
limitation: Laboratory outcomes depend on trading rules and market conditions; thin participation, manipulation, or information asymmetries can change performance substantially.
scenario: Imagine a makerspace exchange where members post both offers to sell surplus wood and bids to buy it, with matched offers producing trades.

title: Barter
finding: Barter exchanges goods or services for other goods or services rather than money. The arrangement requires participants to agree what each side supplies, and may operate directly or through organized exchange networks.
limitation: Avoiding cash does not eliminate valuation disputes or applicable obligations; each party still needs something acceptable to the other.
scenario: Imagine a bicycle mechanic repairing a photographer's bike in exchange for portraits, after they agree on the repair scope and number of finished photographs.

title: Mutual credit
source_title: From an idea to a scalable working model: Sardex
publisher: International Journal of Community Currency Research
finding: Mutual credit records purchases as debits and sales as credits within a participating network. The Sardex case describes an exchange circuit where commercial relationships and trust support transactions alongside the accounting infrastructure.
limitation: A closed circuit needs useful suppliers and credible settlement rules; the Sardex case alone does not establish results for other networks.
scenario: Imagine local workshops accepting account credits for repairs and spending those credits on supplies from other members, within agreed debit limits and a shared ledger.

title: Local currencies
finding: A local currency creates a means of payment accepted by a defined network of businesses and residents. BerkShares illustrates a geographically focused system intended to keep purchasing relationships connected to local enterprises.
limitation: Acceptance, conversion arrangements, and issuer credibility constrain usefulness; local circulation does not by itself demonstrate additional economic activity or equitable benefits.
scenario: Imagine a town introducing vouchers accepted by participating independent shops, with residents checking participating businesses before exchanging money into the local payment system.

title: Gift economies
finding: Gift exchange moves resources through social relationships rather than a price paid at each transfer. Anthropological distinctions between generalized and balanced reciprocity show that gifts can involve very different expectations about returning support.
limitation: Gift practices can carry obligations and status differences; treating every unpaid transfer as unconditional generosity erases important cultural distinctions.
scenario: Imagine neighbors regularly leaving surplus garden produce on a shared table, without tracking equivalent returns, while discussing expectations before the practice expands beyond familiar households.

title: Reciprocal labor exchanges
finding: Reciprocal labor exchanges coordinate help now with an obligation to return help later. The account of Andean ayni describes relationships in which people assist one another when needed and subsequently reciprocate labor.
limitation: Ayni belongs to particular social and cultural relationships; borrowing a work-exchange mechanism does not reproduce those obligations or shared meanings automatically.
scenario: Imagine three households agreeing to help repaint one home each weekend, with the schedule and expected hours discussed before the first household receives assistance.

title: Rotating savings groups
source_title: Indigenous Savings and Credit Societies in the Developing World
publisher: World Bank; F. J. A. Bouman
finding: A rotating savings group collects regular contributions and gives the combined pot to one member each round. Early recipients obtain funds sooner, while later recipients accumulate savings through the same reciprocal commitment.
limitation: Early recipients must keep contributing after receiving their pot; default, unreliable income, and contested ordering can undermine the entire arrangement.
scenario: Imagine six trusted colleagues contributing monthly to a rotating pot, agreeing in advance on the order, missed-payment procedures, and what happens if someone leaves.

title: Credit unions
finding: Credit unions organize financial services through member ownership and member governance. The NCUA describes a cooperative structure with an elected board, linking the institution's users to its ownership rather than external shareholders.
limitation: Member ownership does not remove financial risk or guarantee active participation; regulation and protections vary by jurisdiction and institution.
scenario: Imagine workers considering a member-owned savings institution and comparing its elected governance, membership rules, services, and oversight with other available financial institutions.

title: Mutual insurance
publisher: International Cooperative and Mutual Insurance Federation
finding: Mutual insurance combines pooled protection with policyholder ownership. The practitioner account distinguishes mutual organizations through members' participation in a collective institution, connecting coverage arrangements with governance rather than treating customers solely as purchasers.
limitation: Policyholder ownership does not guarantee adequate reserves, fair claims handling, or equal influence; this practitioner source advocates for its sector.
scenario: Imagine a trade association exploring a member-owned insurer, asking how claims decisions, reserves, elected oversight, and participation would work before choosing any coverage.

title: Emergency mutual-aid funds
finding: An emergency mutual-aid fund collects contributions and redistributes money to people facing immediate hardship. Elswick's published practice uses request rules, available funds, and community review rather than requiring recipients to repay assistance.
limitation: Available money limits support, while eligibility and review rules influence access; one local fund's practice is not a universal governance model.
scenario: Imagine residents pooling donations for neighbors facing sudden utility shutoffs, publishing request criteria and arranging discreet reviews that reveal as little personal information as possible.

title: Crowdfunding
finding: Crowdfunding gathers relatively small contributions from many people through a public campaign or platform. Donation, reward, investment, and lending models create different relationships between contributors, organizers, and any promised return.
limitation: A successful campaign does not guarantee delivery; obligations and exposure differ substantially between donations, rewards, equity participation, and loans.
scenario: Imagine a neighborhood cinema collecting small donations for a projector, explaining its budget, deadline, and what will happen if it raises too little.

title: Crowdlending
finding: Crowdlending connects multiple lenders with borrowers through a platform, with repayment expected rather than a gift. It distributes financing across contributors while making loan terms and platform arrangements central to the relationship.
limitation: Borrowers may default and lenders may be unable to exit; platform involvement does not make repayment or access to funds certain.
scenario: Imagine a workshop comparing a platform loan funded by many lenders with other financing, examining repayment obligations and failure scenarios before accepting any offer.

title: Subscriptions
source_title: Subscription pricing models: A guide for businesses
finding: Subscriptions exchange recurring payments for continuing access or delivery. Different pricing models tie charges to a fixed period, usage, or service tier, creating an ongoing relationship rather than a single purchase.
limitation: Continuing charges require clear cancellation and service expectations; predictable billing for the provider can become unnoticed expenditure for the subscriber.
scenario: Imagine a neighborhood newsletter charging a monthly subscription to fund reporting, specifying publication frequency and providing a straightforward way to cancel before renewal.

title: Membership dues
finding: Membership dues make regular contributions part of belonging to an organization. Rotary's club model illustrates how membership obligations accompany collective activities, distinguishing a continuing association from an occasional donation to a project.
limitation: Dues can exclude people with limited income; the source illustrates one association and does not establish a universally appropriate fee structure.
scenario: Imagine a hiking club setting annual dues to pay for shared equipment, while members debate reduced rates and how the collected money should be reported.

title: Patronage
source_title: Looking to Connect with European Paintings: The Role of the Patron
finding: Patronage connects a creator or institution with a supporter who supplies resources over a project or relationship. Historical commissions show how patrons influenced subjects and opportunities, making support a source of cultural direction.
limitation: Resource dependence can give patrons substantial influence over expression and access; historical commissions illustrate this tension without defining every modern patron relationship.
scenario: Imagine a local business funding a theater's season, with a written understanding of acknowledgement, artistic independence, and whether the supporter can influence programming.

title: Grants
finding: Grants allocate resources to proposed activities through eligibility rules, applications, and assessment. The NEA program illustrates project-based support in which applicants explain intended work and budgets to an external funding body.
limitation: Application capacity and funder priorities shape who receives support; restricted awards can leave necessary operating work or less legible projects unfunded.
scenario: Imagine a community theater applying for support for accessible performances, translating its plan into a budget and checking whether the funder supports the required expenses.

title: Prize competitions
finding: Prize competitions announce a challenge and reward selected solutions after participants develop submissions. The organizer sets the problem and judging criteria, while competitors choose whether to invest effort without a guaranteed award.
limitation: Unsuccessful entrants may receive nothing for substantial work; unclear criteria and ownership terms can deter participation or create disputes.
scenario: Imagine a city offering a prize for a usable flood-warning prototype, publishing evaluation criteria, submission rights, and judging procedures before inviting competing designs.

title: Bounties
source_title: Google Open Source Software Vulnerability Reward Program Rules
finding: Bounties announce rewards for qualifying completed contributions. Google's vulnerability program illustrates a mechanism with defined scope, report requirements, and assessment of submitted findings, connecting payment to an accepted result rather than ongoing employment.
limitation: Ambiguous scope, duplicate discoveries, and discretionary evaluation can leave contributors unpaid; security-report rules are specific to the program issuing them.
scenario: Imagine a software project posting a reward for reproducing a particular bug, defining the evidence required and how duplicate submissions will be handled.

title: Quadratic funding
source_title: A Flexible Design for Funding Public Goods
finding: Quadratic funding calculates support using the square of the sum of square roots of contributions. This makes the distribution depend on how many people contribute, with outside subsidy supporting broadly backed projects.
limitation: Identity duplication, collusion, and finite subsidy budgets complicate implementation; theoretical efficiency depends on assumptions that real funding communities may not satisfy.
scenario: Imagine a town testing matching funds for public projects, comparing how many distinct residents support each proposal and publishing safeguards against coordinated fake donations.

title: Matching grants
finding: Matching grants make an award conditional on obtaining additional eligible resources. The NEA example permits specified matching contributions, linking external funding with resources that an applicant or other supporters must bring.
limitation: Organizations with wealthier networks can find matching requirements easier; eligible cash and in-kind contributions depend on the particular funder's rules.
scenario: Imagine a youth music group offered funding if it secures other eligible contributions, then checking whether donated venue time counts before promising its match.

title: Endowments
finding: An endowment holds invested assets to support continuing institutional activity through distributions over time. Harvard's account distinguishes ongoing spending needs from preserving resources for the future, with many gifts restricted to particular purposes.
limitation: Investment losses and spending rules constrain available support; a large asset balance does not imply unrestricted money for any current priority.
scenario: Imagine a small museum establishing a long-term conservation fund, distinguishing what donors restrict from what annual operations need and deciding how distributions will be governed.

title: Pooled procurement
finding: Pooled procurement coordinates orders from multiple purchasers through shared purchasing arrangements. The Global Fund's procedures connect requests, financing, approvals, and delivery, turning separate demand into a managed procurement process with common requirements.
limitation: Pooling requires compatible specifications, reliable payment, and coordination; larger orders alone cannot guarantee timely delivery or eliminate supplier dependence.
scenario: Imagine several clinics combining orders for identical supplies, agreeing on specifications, funding responsibilities, delivery schedules, and what happens when one participant changes its request.

title: Buying clubs
source_title: America's Farms and Ranches at a Glance: 2022 Edition
finding: Buying clubs organize participants to purchase inputs together. The USDA account identifies organizations formed to manage farm purchases, illustrating how members can coordinate demand without transferring the whole management of their enterprises.
limitation: Members must align quantities, payment, and distribution; a purchasing club can create administrative work even when it negotiates attractive prices.
scenario: Imagine five small farms grouping fertilizer orders, choosing a coordinator and agreeing on payment deadlines and collection responsibilities before asking suppliers for quotations.

title: Tool libraries
finding: Tool libraries provide temporary access to a shared inventory rather than requiring each user to own equipment. Seattle REconomy's rules illustrate borrowing periods, returns, renewals, and training requirements that keep lending workable.
limitation: Maintenance, safe use, and overdue items require ongoing coordination; a catalog listing does not guarantee a tool is available when needed.
scenario: Imagine neighbors borrowing a drill for a weekend shelf installation, completing any required orientation and returning it on time for the next person's reservation.

title: Resource booking systems
finding: Resource booking systems assign access to a shared resource for specified periods. The university simulator example combines reservations with eligibility, time limits, and arrival procedures so competing users can plan use.
limitation: No-shows and overbooking waste capacity; published reservations need workable cancellation, access, and enforcement rules rather than merely a shared calendar.
scenario: Imagine a community studio booking its recording booth in two-hour blocks, releasing unclaimed slots after a grace period and displaying availability to all members.

title: Queues
finding: Queues allocate access through an ordered sequence of people waiting for service or a limited resource. Wimbledon's numbered, nontransferable queue cards illustrate how an organization makes waiting order visible and prevents place transfers.
limitation: Waiting imposes unequal costs on people with different schedules and mobility; orderly access does not make the underlying allocation universally fair.
scenario: Imagine a neighborhood repair event assigning arrival numbers, explaining priority exceptions and letting people step away while they wait for their turn.

title: Allocation lotteries
publisher: Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea
finding: Allocation lotteries use random selection to choose among eligible claimants when demand exceeds supply. The admissions example describes supervised random allocation, separating eligibility rules from the random ordering of qualifying applications.
limitation: Random selection equalizes chances only within the eligible pool; eligibility design and transparent administration still determine who can benefit.
scenario: Imagine a workshop with twenty seats and fifty eligible applicants, publishing its eligibility rules before drawing places randomly and maintaining a waiting list.

title: Needs-based allocation
finding: Needs-based allocation directs assistance according to assessed urgency or deprivation. UNHCR's principle of impartiality prioritizes acute protection risks and urgent needs rather than political affiliation, making assessment criteria central to distribution.
limitation: Assessments can miss hidden needs or impose intrusive disclosure; impartial intent requires accessible processes and revision when circumstances change.
scenario: Imagine a neighborhood relief group distributing limited heaters first to households facing the most urgent exposure, with a private request route and reassessment process.

title: Rationing
source_title: Connecting, Sharing, Learning: Second World War
finding: Rationing sets limits on how much of a scarce resource people may obtain. Britain's wartime food system used ration books and coupons to administer allowances rather than leaving access entirely to purchasing power.
limitation: Historical allowances do not establish an ideal contemporary distribution; enforcement, differential needs, and informal markets can complicate equal-looking quotas.
scenario: Imagine a campsite facing a temporary water shortage setting daily allowances, explaining essential-use exceptions and tracking supplies until normal access can resume.

title: Tradable quotas
finding: Tradable quotas divide a regulated allowance into rights that eligible holders can transfer. NOAA distinguishes transferable fishing quotas from other catch-share arrangements, showing how an overall limit can coexist with exchange between participants.
limitation: Allocation choices affect who benefits, and transfers can concentrate control; a quota system still needs credible limits, monitoring, and enforcement.
scenario: Imagine a regulated fishery comparing transferable catch shares with nontransferable allocations, examining how initial distribution and ownership limits would affect small operators.

title: Employee ownership
finding: Employee ownership gives workers an ownership stake in the enterprise employing them. The NCEO introduction illustrates one particular vehicle, the employee stock ownership plan, rather than equating every ownership arrangement with worker self-government.
limitation: An ownership stake does not automatically confer equal voting power or workplace control; the cited ESOP model is jurisdiction-specific.
scenario: Imagine a retiring owner discussing a worker ownership transition, explicitly separating questions about financial stakes, board selection, everyday management, and the risks employees would bear.

title: Steward ownership
finding: Steward ownership separates control of a company from unrestricted financial extraction or resale. Purpose describes arrangements intended to keep decision authority connected to the enterprise's mission while directing profits toward its continued purpose.
limitation: Implementation varies by legal structure and governance design; locking in a mission does not guarantee that stewards remain accountable or competent.
scenario: Imagine a mission-driven manufacturer exploring a succession structure that preserves its purpose, asking who appoints future stewards and how those stewards can be replaced.

title: Revenue sharing
finding: Revenue sharing divides incoming sales receipts according to an agreed arrangement before treating them as one party's exclusive income. Bandcamp illustrates a platform taking a stated share while the remainder reaches artists or labels.
limitation: Revenue differs from profit; costs, processing charges, refunds, and reporting rules determine what a stated percentage actually delivers to participants.
scenario: Imagine a musician and venue agreeing how ticket receipts will be divided, separately specifying payment processing, refunds, and whether production costs come out first.

title: Profit sharing
source_title: Our Profit-Sharing and Charitable Contributions Formula
finding: Profit sharing distributes part of an organization's surplus to participants using a stated formula. Buffer's account links a team bonus pool to annual net income, distinguishing profit-based distributions from sharing gross sales revenue.
limitation: Accounting choices and distribution rules affect payouts; a profitable period is not assured, and bonuses do not substitute for participation in governance.
scenario: Imagine a small firm allocating part of annual surplus to staff, explaining its accounting basis and distribution formula before anyone relies on a possible bonus.

title: Transparent compensation formulas
source_title: The Next Evolution of Transparent Salaries
finding: Transparent compensation formulas make the factors used to set pay visible and explainable. Buffer's account describes revising a formula when complexity and subjective decisions weakened the intended consistency of its compensation approach.
limitation: Public formulas still embed judgments about roles, benchmarks, and location; transparency makes these choices inspectable rather than automatically equitable.
scenario: Imagine a nonprofit publishing how role level and experience affect salary, then giving staff a process to question their classification and suggest revisions.

title: Rent allocation formulas
finding: Rent allocation formulas divide a total housing cost across occupants or rooms using explicit criteria. Spliddit's example uses reported room valuations to find an assignment in which occupants do not prefer another room-price combination.
limitation: Fairness guarantees depend on the model and reported valuations; budget constraints, relationships, and changing preferences may require additional negotiation.
scenario: Imagine three housemates valuing differently sized bedrooms, comparing a calculated rent division with their budgets, then agreeing how future room swaps will be handled.

title: Fiscal sponsorship
finding: Fiscal sponsorship places a project's administrative and financial oversight within an existing nonprofit organization. The sponsor assumes specified responsibilities for mission-related work while project leaders carry out activities under the agreed arrangement.
limitation: Sponsorship includes real oversight and liabilities, not merely passing donations through; control, fees, and separation arrangements require clear agreement.
scenario: Imagine a new community archive operating through an established nonprofit while testing demand, agreeing how funds, reporting, staff responsibilities, and eventual independence would be managed.

title: Community-supported agriculture
finding: Community-supported agriculture connects consumers and growers through advance commitments to a farm's production. The USDA description emphasizes shared support and exposure to production outcomes, linking consumption with the farm's continuing operation.
limitation: Models vary in how much harvest risk members actually share; an advance payment does not necessarily imply ownership or farm governance.
scenario: Imagine households subscribing to a farm's seasonal produce share, clarifying delivery arrangements and what happens if weather reduces the harvest before making their commitment.

title: Repair cafés
finding: Repair cafés bring people, broken possessions, tools, and volunteer expertise together to attempt repairs collaboratively. Participants learn through working alongside repairers, combining practical reuse with an accessible occasion for local social contact.
limitation: Volunteer expertise and available parts limit what can be repaired; collaborative repair needs appropriate safety practices and realistic expectations about success.
scenario: Imagine residents meeting monthly at a library to repair lamps and clothing together, with volunteers checking which jobs can safely be attempted on site.

title: Swap events
source_title: What you buy, use and dispose of
finding: Swap events gather unwanted but usable goods so participants can exchange or redistribute them. Westminster's examples include recurring community exchanges for clothing, books, toys, and baby equipment, organized around practical local reuse.
limitation: Incoming goods need suitability checks and leftover plans; requiring equal-value exchanges can exclude participants who have little to contribute.
scenario: Imagine a school holding a uniform exchange before term begins, explaining acceptable condition, whether donations are required, and where unclaimed clothing will go.

title: Escrow
finding: Escrow places money, documents, or other assets with a third party until specified conditions are met. It coordinates an exchange by separating possession of the asset from either party's unilateral control during completion.
limitation: The arrangement depends on trustworthy administration and clear release conditions; disputed performance can still require an agreed resolution process.
scenario: Imagine two organizations exchanging a commissioned digital archive, considering a neutral holding arrangement that releases payment only after the explicitly agreed delivery conditions are verified.

title: Contracts
finding: Contracts create agreements whose obligations can be enforced through a legal system. The Cornell account explains how mutual commitments acquire legal consequences, distinguishing an enforceable agreement from every informal promise people make.
limitation: Enforceability depends on applicable law and the agreement's circumstances; written detail cannot anticipate every contingency or erase unequal bargaining power.
scenario: Imagine a community venue commissioning renovations and documenting the scope, payment stages, change process, and dispute arrangements before either side begins substantial work.

title: Copyleft
finding: Copyleft uses copyright licensing to preserve recipients' freedoms when covered work is redistributed or modified. GNU explains the mechanism as requiring downstream distribution to retain specified permissions rather than allowing redistribution to strip them away.
limitation: Specific licenses differ in scope and obligations; copyleft does not mean abandoning copyright or automatically requiring publication of every private modification.
scenario: Imagine a software collective choosing a copyleft license so distributed improvements remain available under its sharing terms, checking compatibility before combining existing components.

title: Public provisioning
source_title: What Goals Should We Seek in Politics?
finding: Public provisioning organizes government responsibility for supplying services or resources. OpenStax illustrates why collective financing can support goods such as street lighting when individual transactions cannot readily recover the costs from everyone benefiting.
limitation: Publicly supplied services are not all economic public goods; financing, delivery, eligibility, and accountability remain separate choices within public provision.
scenario: Imagine a municipality arranging street lighting for an underserved district, deciding how to fund maintenance and how residents can report failures or challenge uneven coverage.

title: Certification
finding: Certification provides a third party's assurance that a specified product, service, or system meets stated requirements. ISO distinguishes developing standards from issuing certificates, which independent certification bodies perform within a defined assessment scope.
limitation: A certificate supports a specific conformity claim, not unlimited competence or quality; readers must check its scope, issuer, and status.
scenario: Imagine a purchaser comparing suppliers' certificates, checking which processes each certificate covers and whether the issuing body and assessment remain relevant to the purchase.

title: Accreditation
finding: Accreditation evaluates the competence of organizations that conduct specified assessments. In ISO's explanation, an independent accreditation body recognizes a certification body's operation against standards, adding another level of scrutiny to certification claims.
limitation: Accreditation applies to an identified scope and body; it is not a personal skill credential or a guarantee against every failure.
scenario: Imagine a laboratory customer checking whether the laboratory's accreditation covers the particular testing method required, rather than treating an accreditation logo as a universal endorsement.

title: Professional licensing
finding: Professional licensing makes permission to practice an occupation contingent on requirements set by an authorized regulator. CareerOneStop distinguishes such permission from voluntary certification, while noting that requirements vary across jurisdictions and occupations.
limitation: Legal authorization is not proof of consistently excellent performance; licensing requirements and portability depend on the relevant jurisdiction and occupation.
scenario: Imagine someone comparing pathways into a regulated trade, checking the actual regulator's requirements and distinguishing required permission from optional training certificates offered by private providers.

title: Portfolios
finding: Portfolios present selected examples of previous work for others to inspect and discuss. Oxford's interview guidance describes using those examples to explore creative work in depth rather than relying solely on qualifications or verbal claims.
limitation: Selected work can obscure collaboration, context, or failed attempts; reviewers need to establish the applicant's contribution and the relevance of each example.
scenario: Imagine a community group choosing a designer by reviewing previous posters together, asking who produced each element and how the designer handled constraints and revisions.

title: References
finding: References obtain information from people familiar with a candidate's past work. OPM recommends structured questions tied to job requirements and consistent recording, turning informal endorsements into more comparable evidence for a selection decision.
limitation: Referees may be selective, reluctant, or biased; consistent questions improve comparability but cannot make every account complete or independent.
scenario: Imagine a hiring panel asking each candidate's former collaborators the same questions about relevant responsibilities, recording concrete examples rather than simply counting enthusiastic recommendations.

title: Reputation systems
publisher: Communications of the ACM; Resnick, Zeckhauser, Friedman, Kuwabara
finding: Reputation systems collect and communicate information about past interactions so unfamiliar participants can judge whom to trust. The research describes online systems as a way to carry reputational information beyond direct personal acquaintance.
limitation: Feedback can be manipulated or biased toward visible participants; a score may conceal context, changing behavior, or people excluded from participation.
scenario: Imagine an equipment-sharing network displaying completed loans and contextual feedback, allowing disputes to be reviewed instead of reducing every borrower to an unexplained number.

title: Contribution records
finding: Contribution records preserve traces of participation for later inspection. GitHub's profile documentation illustrates timelines of commits, pull requests, and issues, while distinguishing visible public activity from private work whose details may remain hidden.
limitation: Recorded activity is not equivalent to impact or quality; private work, maintenance, mentoring, and excluded contribution types may be underrepresented.
scenario: Imagine a volunteer project reviewing a person's documented contributions before offering responsibilities, examining the work itself and asking about important contributions that its tracking system missed.

title: Contributor credits
finding: Contributor credits publicly acknowledge people and the kinds of work they provided. The All Contributors specification uses prominent contributor lists and contribution categories to recognize work that conventional code-focused records can overlook.
limitation: Credit categories can still omit invisible labor; acknowledgement does not itself confer payment, decision rights, or agreement about relative contribution.
scenario: Imagine an open-source project crediting documentation, accessibility testing, event organization, and code contributions together, inviting contributors to correct omissions before each release is published.

title: Authorship conventions
source_title: Defining the Role of Authors and Contributors
publisher: International Committee of Medical Journal Editors
finding: Authorship conventions specify who qualifies for a byline and what responsibility accompanies it. ICMJE distinguishes authors from other acknowledged contributors through combined criteria, connecting recognition with participation, approval, and accountability for the work.
limitation: Disciplinary conventions differ; formal criteria cannot settle disputes without transparent discussion, and seniority or funding alone does not establish authorship.
scenario: Imagine a research team discussing authorship roles before writing begins, revisiting them as contributions change and acknowledging substantial help that does not meet its agreed criteria.

title: Merit-based selection
finding: Merit-based selection defines advancement around relevant abilities, knowledge, and skills assessed through open competition. The cited civil-service principles frame this as a procedural commitment to fair opportunity, rather than deference to political allegiance.
limitation: What counts as merit remains a design choice; credentials and test scores can reflect unequal opportunity rather than relevant demonstrated capability.
scenario: Imagine a cooperative recruiting an operations lead, defining necessary tasks and evaluating applicants against the same evidence criteria instead of choosing the best-connected member.

title: Seniority rules
source_title: Public Service Orders: Seniority on Promotion
publisher: Government of Seychelles; ILO NATLEX archive
finding: Seniority rules establish priority using time in a role or another specified service measure. The cited public-service orders illustrate formal ordering by promotion date, showing how an explicit rule can structure otherwise discretionary comparisons.
limitation: Different systems calculate seniority differently; length of service does not necessarily measure present capability or justify every allocation of opportunity.
scenario: Imagine a volunteer venue allocating preferred shifts by a published service-length rule, debating exceptions for accessibility and whether newer members should receive a minimum share.

title: Competitive examinations
finding: Competitive examinations compare candidates through a defined assessment process for entry into positions or candidate pools. The UN program combines an entrance examination with subsequent professional development, making examination one stage within recruitment.
limitation: Exam performance captures only selected abilities; eligibility restrictions, preparation access, and later appointment processes limit what passing an examination establishes.
scenario: Imagine a public organization recruiting analysts through a published examination, checking that the exercises resemble relevant work and explaining what successful candidates can expect afterward.

title: Work-sample assessments
finding: Work-sample assessments ask candidates to perform tasks resembling the work being selected for. OPM describes simulations and exercises that provide direct evidence of relevant behavior, rather than inferring competence solely from background information.
limitation: Work samples can unfairly test skills intended to be taught after entry; realistic tasks also require careful design and consistent assessment.
scenario: Imagine a nonprofit hiring an event coordinator by asking applicants to resolve the same fictional scheduling conflict, using a common rubric and a reasonable time limit.

title: Auditions
finding: Auditions evaluate performed ability through specified demonstrations before selectors. The Tanglewood chorus example combines prepared music, rhythm, scales, and diction, showing how a short performance can sample several requirements of participation.
limitation: Brief performances are sensitive to nerves and preparation access; selectors must decide which qualities the audition can actually reveal.
scenario: Imagine a community ensemble inviting singers to prepare the same excerpt and a personal selection, explaining criteria and accommodation options before assigning audition times.

title: Trial projects
finding: Trial projects let both sides experience a bounded piece of working together before a longer commitment. Automattic describes paid, part-time trials used to evaluate work, communication, effectiveness, and mutual compatibility.
limitation: Trials can burden applicants with existing obligations; clear payment, scope, evaluation, and ownership arrangements are necessary to avoid extracting unpaid work.
scenario: Imagine a small design studio commissioning a paid, limited trial project, agreeing on hours and evaluation criteria so the candidate can also assess collaboration.

title: Blind review
finding: Blind review withholds selected identity information from evaluators while they assess work. Nature Health's double-anonymous option requires authors to conceal identifying material, making anonymity an operational preparation task rather than simply a promise.
limitation: Subject matter, references, or public drafts can reveal identity; anonymity does not remove all bias or substitute for relevant evaluation criteria.
scenario: Imagine a writing competition removing names and biographical details before judging, asking entrants to flag identifying content and documenting how reviewers handle accidental recognition.

title: Sponsorship for advancement
finding: Sponsorship for advancement involves an influential person advocating for someone else's opportunities. Catalyst distinguishes this relationship from guidance alone, focusing on access to networks and people willing to support another person's progression.
limitation: Sponsorship can reproduce favoritism when access is informal; transparent opportunities and scrutiny of whose talent receives advocacy remain necessary.
scenario: Imagine a senior colleague putting a capable junior forward for a visible project, explaining the relevant evidence and ensuring others also have routes to consideration.

title: Deputy roles
finding: Deputy roles distribute leadership responsibilities and provide continuity when a primary leader is unavailable or leaves. Bridgespan's COO account describes interim leadership and preserved relationships without assuming that every deputy becomes the permanent successor.
limitation: Unclear authority can create competing leadership centers; a deputy's operational effectiveness does not automatically make them the appropriate next leader.
scenario: Imagine a community center designating a deputy to handle defined decisions during the director's absence, documenting escalation limits and separately planning any permanent succession.

title: Founder transition agreements
source_title: Leadership Transition: Overcoming the Threat of Founder's Syndrome
finding: Founder transition agreements clarify what a departing founder may continue doing and what passes to successors. INTRAC emphasizes board responsibility and explicit boundaries when founders remain involved, reducing ambiguity around continuing influence.
limitation: A written boundary cannot ensure compliance; successor authority and independent board oversight matter when a founder retains strong informal relationships.
scenario: Imagine a nonprofit founder remaining available for donor introductions after stepping down, with the board specifying reporting relationships, decision limits, and a review date.

title: Emeritus roles
finding: Emeritus roles distinguish past contribution from current active participation. Apache's published process lets members move into emeritus status and describes a route back through election, making the status a defined governance category.
limitation: Emeritus titles differ across institutions; honorary recognition must not leave unclear whether former leaders retain votes, access, or operational authority.
scenario: Imagine a long-serving association organizer stepping into an honorary advisory role, with members documenting which responsibilities end and how any future return would be decided.

title: Exit interviews
finding: Exit interviews ask departing participants about their experience and reasons for leaving. Glasgow's guidance explores role expectations and communication, turning departure into a chance to identify conditions that current participants may hesitate to discuss.
limitation: Departing people may still fear consequences or withhold criticism; collecting feedback is useful only if patterns receive credible follow-up.
scenario: Imagine a volunteer coordinator offering a departing organizer a private conversation about workload and collaboration, explaining who will see the notes and how recurring issues will be addressed.

title: Backup ownership
finding: Backup ownership gives more than one trusted person the access needed to keep a shared project operating. The Open Source Guides recommend organizational accounts and a backup administrator to reduce dependence on one individual.
limitation: Additional access creates security and accountability responsibilities; a nominal backup is ineffective if permissions, knowledge, or availability are never checked.
scenario: Imagine a volunteer website adding a second authorized administrator, testing recovery access and documenting renewal responsibilities before the original maintainer leaves for several months.

title: Lineage recognition
finding: Lineage recognition locates a person's recognized role within a chain of teachers and predecessors. San Francisco Zen Center's account names a teacher's Dharma transmission and lineage, making continuity part of how authority is described.
limitation: Lineage recognition has tradition-specific meanings; it is neither a universal competence test nor a guarantee that a recognized teacher behaves responsibly.
scenario: Imagine a practitioner choosing a study community and asking how it understands teacher lineage, while separately examining teaching conduct, accountability arrangements, and suitability for their needs.

title: Oaths of office
finding: Oaths of office mark entry into a role through an explicit commitment to its duties or governing order. The Senate's history shows an institutionalized promise whose wording has changed with political circumstances.
limitation: A solemn promise cannot enforce itself; accountability still depends on institutions, review, and consequences when the officeholder violates their duties.
scenario: Imagine a newly elected association board publicly affirming its responsibilities and conflict rules at the start of a term, while explaining the mechanisms members can use to challenge misconduct.

title: Citizen science
finding: Citizen science organizes public participation in a research process rather than limiting research activity to professional scientists. The toolkit connects scoping, project design, community building, data management, and sustaining the effort as interdependent tasks.
limitation: Participation alone does not ensure reliable data or shared authority; project design determines contributors’ roles, quality controls, and access to results.
scenario: Hypothetically, residents could follow a common protocol to record local bird sightings, review uncertain identifications, and contribute observations to a shared dataset used by researchers.

title: Participatory mapping
finding: Participatory mapping lets community members represent places, resources, and land relationships using their own knowledge. Choices about the map’s purpose, audience, and ownership determine whether the process serves community priorities or external demands.
limitation: A published map can expose sensitive places or disputed claims; maps remain selective representations and do not automatically settle ownership.
scenario: Hypothetically, residents could map routes to water points and seasonal obstacles, decide which information should remain private, and use the agreed map to discuss maintenance priorities.

title: Deliberative polling
finding: Deliberative polling brings a sampled public into informed, facilitated discussion and compares opinions before and after deliberation. Its purpose is to examine considered public judgment under specified conditions, not simply collect immediate reactions.
limitation: A deliberative poll is not automatically a binding vote; recruitment, information balance, participation, and question design affect what the results support.
scenario: Hypothetically, a city could recruit a representative sample to examine transport options, question competing experts, discuss tradeoffs, and compare participants’ preferences before and after the event.

title: Congregations
finding: Congregations can organize continuing mutual support alongside religious participation. The National Congregations Study explicitly examines designated people or committees helping members, as well as organized social-service and neighborhood work, making these activities distinct from merely sharing worship space.
limitation: The codebook establishes what the study measures, not how common or effective each activity is; congregations vary greatly in organization.
scenario: Hypothetically, a congregation could maintain a volunteer coordinator who matches members’ offers of rides and meals with requests, while keeping participation voluntary and recipients’ preferences central.

title: Pilgrimage
source_title: Pilgrimage to the St. Thaddeus Apostle Monastery
finding: Pilgrimage combines travel to a meaningful destination with shared practice and temporary proximity. UNESCO’s monastery example describes gathering, procession, worship, food, and camping, showing how a journey can also organize relationships and cultural transmission.
limitation: This describes a specific Armenian Christian heritage practice; secular journeys are analogies, and pilgrimage meanings cannot be reduced to social bonding.
scenario: Hypothetically, members of a faith community could travel together to an important sanctuary, prepare newcomers beforehand, and share time for reflection and community meals along the route.

title: Mutual-benefit societies
finding: Mutual-benefit societies pool members’ contributions to provide assistance under agreed conditions.
